# Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test {#sec-km}

```{r}
#| label: setup-ch2
#| include: false
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(dplyr)
library(broom)
source("R/pairwise_logrank.R")
lung <- survival::lung |>
  mutate(status = status - 1,
         sex = factor(sex, 1:2, c("Male", "Female")))
```

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## In this chapter
**The question.** Did women with advanced lung cancer survive longer than men?

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to:**

- explain how the **Kaplan–Meier** estimator builds a survival curve, and how it handles censored patients;
- fit and plot KM curves in R, and read off median survival and survival at chosen times;
- describe the **hazard** in plain words;
- compare groups with the **log-rank test**, and follow up three or more groups with adjusted pairwise tests.
:::

## Warm-up: remember Chapter 1? {.unnumbered}

Two quick questions to bring back the key ideas from last time.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz([
 {
  "q": "A patient was still alive when the study closed, after 3 years of follow-up. How is this recorded?",
  "options": [
   "Event at 3 years",
   "Censored at 3 years",
   "Excluded from the analysis",
   "Recorded as missing"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "They were event-free for 3 years, and we don't know what happened after that: time = 3, status = 0 (censored).",
  "hints": [
   "No event happened, so status must be 0.",
   "",
   "Excluding them throws away 3 years of event-free follow-up.",
   "Censored data aren't missing. They tell us the patient survived at least 3 years."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "Which assumption about censoring do the methods in this book rely on?",
  "options": [
   "There is no censoring",
   "Censoring is non-informative: censored patients have the same future risk as those still followed",
   "Censoring only happens at the end of the study",
   "Each group has the same amount of censoring"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "Censoring can happen at any time, and groups can differ in how much there is. What matters is that censoring isn't related to a patient's risk.",
  "hints": [
   "Survival methods exist precisely *because* there is censoring.",
   "",
   "Drop-outs during the study are fine, as long as they aren't related to risk.",
   "Groups can have different amounts of censoring."
  ]
 }
])
```

## The idea

The **survival function** $S(t)$ is the probability of being event-free
beyond time $t$. Survival curves always start at $S(0) = 1$ and can only
go down.

The **Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator** is named after Edward Kaplan and Paul
Meier, who published it in 1958 [@kaplan1958]. Its other name, the
*product-limit estimator*, describes how it works: the curve is the
**product** of the chances of surviving each step. It splits follow-up
into steps at each time an event happens. At each event time $t_j$:

- $n_j$ = number **at risk** just before $t_j$. These are people who have
  not had the event and have not yet been censored.
- $d_j$ = number of **events** at $t_j$.
- The chance of surviving that step, given you got that far, is
  $1 - d_j / n_j$.

Survival to time $t$ is the product of all the steps so far:

$$
\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)
$$

Censored people **count in the risk set until they are censored**, and then
leave quietly. They never count as an event. This is how KM uses the partial
information from censored people.

## Interactive app: Kaplan–Meier by hand {#sec-app-km-hand}

Type survival times separated by commas, and add `+` to mark a censored
time. Edit the data and watch the table and curve update. Try adding a
censored time *before* the first event, or a tie (two events at the same
time).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {kmFit, kmMedian, logrank, makeRandom, nAtRisk, quiz} from "./js/survtools.js"
```

::: {.app}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kmText = Inputs.text({label: "Times (+ = censored)", value: "2, 3+, 4, 4, 6+, 7, 9, 11+, 13, 15+", width: 420})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kmParsed = kmText.split(/[,\s]+/).filter(s => s.length).map(s => ({
  time: parseFloat(s), event: s.trim().endsWith("+") ? 0 : 1
})).filter(d => !isNaN(d.time) && d.time >= 0)
kmHand = kmFit(kmParsed.map(d => d.time), kmParsed.map(d => d.event))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(kmHand.slice(1).map(r => ({
  "Time t": r.time,
  "At risk (n)": r.nrisk,
  "Events (d)": r.nevent,
  "Censored": r.ncens,
  "Step: 1 − d/n": r.nevent ? `1 − ${r.nevent}/${r.nrisk} = ${(1 - r.nevent / r.nrisk).toFixed(3)}` : "1 (no event)",
  "S(t)": r.surv.toFixed(3)
})), {layout: "auto", rows: 20})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  height: 300, y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Survival probability S(t)", grid: true},
  x: {label: "Time →"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(kmHand, {x: "time", y: "surv", curve: "step-after", strokeWidth: 2.5, stroke: "#0072B2"}),
    Plot.dot(kmHand.filter(r => r.ncens > 0), {x: "time", y: "surv", symbol: "plus", r: 6, stroke: "#0072B2", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#D55E00", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.text([`Median = ${isNaN(kmMedian(kmHand)) ? "not reached" : kmMedian(kmHand)}`],
      {frameAnchor: "top-right", dy: 5, dx: -5, fill: "#D55E00"})
  ]
})
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding
- Why doesn't the curve drop at a censored time (`+`)?
- After a censored observation, why are the drops at later events
  *bigger*?
- What happens to the median if the last observation is censored and
  $S(t)$ never goes below 0.5?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answers
Using the default data (`2, 3+, 4, 4, 6+, 7, 9, 11+, 13, 15+`):

- **No drop at a censored time.** No event happened there. The censored
  person just leaves the risk set, so $d = 0$ and the step factor is
  $1 - 0/n = 1$. Look at time 3: $S(t)$ stays at 0.900.
- **Bigger drops later.** Each censored person who leaves makes the risk
  set smaller, so each later death is a larger *fraction* of the people
  still at risk. The single death at time 2 removes 1/10 of the survival
  probability (10 at risk). The single death at time 13 removes **half**
  of it, because only 2 people are left at risk. This is also why the
  right-hand end of a KM curve is so uncertain.
- **Median never reached.** The median is the first time $S(t) \le 0.5$.
  Here it is 9. If the curve never drops to 0.5, for example because the
  last observations are censored (try `2, 3+, 4, 6+, 9+, 11+`), the median
  is **not reached**. R prints `NA`. Don't report the last follow-up time
  instead. Report "not reached", and give survival at fixed time points or
  the lower confidence limit for the median if it's available.
:::

## Kaplan–Meier in R

`survfit()` fits the KM estimator. `~ 1` means one curve for everyone.

```{r}
#| label: km-overall
km_all <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)
km_all
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## How to read this output
- **n**: patients (228). **events**: deaths (165).
- **median**: the median survival time, 310 days. Half the patients had
  died by then.
- **0.95LCL, 0.95UCL**: the lower and upper limits of the 95% confidence
  interval for the median (285 to 363 days).
:::

`summary()` gives the estimated survival at times you choose. Here we
use 180, 365 and 730 days (6 months, 1 year, 2 years):

```{r}
#| label: km-summary
summary(km_all, times = c(180, 365, 730))
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## How to read this output
One row per chosen time:

- **n.risk**: patients still alive and in follow-up at that time.
- **n.event**: deaths since the previous time shown.
- **survival**: the estimated proportion still alive, $\hat S(t)$.
- **lower/upper 95% CI**: its confidence interval. (`std.err` is the
  standard error, which you rarely need.)
:::

So about 41% of patients (95% CI 34%–49%) were still alive at one year.

### Plotting with `ggsurvfit`

The **ggsurvfit** package makes good KM plots that work with ggplot2. Use
`survfit2()` instead of `survfit()`. It is identical, but it remembers the
data and variable labels for plotting.

```{r}
#| label: fig-km-overall
#| fig-cap: "Overall Kaplan–Meier curve for the lung cancer data."
survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_censor_mark(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250)) +
  labs(x = "Days since enrolment", y = "Overall survival probability")
```

The **risk table** under the plot shows how many patients are still being
followed. Always include it. The right-hand end of a KM curve is usually
based on very few people, so read it with caution.

## Comparing groups

Put a grouping variable on the right-hand side of the formula:

```{r}
#| label: km-sex
km_sex <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
km_sex
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-km-sex
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan–Meier curves by sex."
km_sex |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  add_pvalue(location = "annotation", x = 750) +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Days since enrolment")
```

The women's curve stays above the men's: at every point in time, a higher
proportion of women were still alive. Is that difference bigger than we'd
expect by chance? Before answering that, we need one new idea.

### A first look at the hazard {#sec-hazard-intro}

So far we've described survival as the **proportion still alive** at
each time. Another way to describe it is the **hazard**: *the risk of the
event right now, for someone who has survived so far*.

::: {.callout-note}
## The hazard in plain words
Imagine 100 patients are still alive at the start of month 6, and 5 of
them die during month 6. The hazard in month 6 is roughly
**5 per 100 per month**: the death rate among the people still at risk.

- The **survival curve** answers: *what proportion are still alive at time t?*
- The **hazard** answers: *among those still alive, how fast are the
  events happening right now?*

A **hazard ratio (HR)** compares the hazards of two groups. For example,
HR = 0.6 for treatment B vs treatment A means that, at any moment, patients
on B are dying at 60% of the rate of patients on A. HR = 1 means no
difference.

Chapter 3 covers hazards and hazard ratios properly. For now, "hazard ≈
death rate among those still alive" is all you need.
:::

### The log-rank test {#sec-logrank}

The **log-rank test** asks whether the survival curves are the same. At
every time a death occurs, it compares the number of deaths in each group
with the number we'd **expect** if both groups had the same hazard. Then it
adds up the differences over all those times.

```{r}
#| label: logrank
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## How to read this output
- **N**: patients in each group.
- **Observed**: deaths that actually happened in each group.
- **Expected**: deaths we'd expect in each group if men and women had
  the same hazard.
- `(O-E)^2/E` and `(O-E)^2/V`: intermediate steps in the calculation.
  You can ignore them.
- **Chisq … p**: the test result. This is the line you report.
:::

Men had 112 deaths when about 91.6 were expected. Women had 53 when about
73.4 were expected. Men died more often than expected and women less often.
The test gives $\chi^2 = 10.3$ on 1 degree of freedom, $p = 0.001$, so there
is strong evidence that survival differed by sex.

::: {.callout-warning}
## What the log-rank test can't do
- It gives a **p-value only**. It doesn't say *how big* the difference is.
  For that we need a hazard ratio (Chapter 3).
- It works best when one group's hazard is a constant multiple of the
  other's. If the curves **cross**, it can miss a real difference.
- It does **not adjust for other variables**. In observational data, a
  difference in KM curves may be due to confounding (Chapters 5–7).
:::

### Practice: fill in the blanks

*This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.*

Do patients aged 70 or over survive less long than younger patients? Replace
each `______` with the right code, then click **Run Code**.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_km_age
library(survival)
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1        # recode to 0 = censored, 1 = died
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_km_age
#| caption: "Practice: KM curves by age group"
# TRUE for patients aged 70 or over
lung$old <- lung$age >= ______

# One curve per age group, and the median in each
fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ ______, data = lung)
print(fit)

# Survival at 1 year (time is in days)
summary(fit, times = ______)

# Log-rank test
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ______, data = lung)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_km_age"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1
The new column is called `old`, so that is the grouping variable on the
right of each `~`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_km_age"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2
The age cut-off is `70`. Time in `lung` is measured in days, so one year is
`365`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_km_age"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
lung$old <- lung$age >= 70

fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ old, data = lung)
print(fit)
summary(fit, times = 365)
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ old, data = lung)
```

Median survival was 283 days for patients aged 70 or over (`old=TRUE`) and
340 days for younger patients. At one year, about 30% of the older group and
45% of the younger group were still alive. The difference is just
significant: log-rank $\chi^2 = 4.0$ on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.04.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_km_age
#| check: true
env <- .envir_result
if (is.null(env$lung$old)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
       message = "First create the <code>old</code> column: replace the first blank with the age cut-off.")
} else if (!identical(env$lung$old, survival::lung$age >= 70)) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "Check the age cut-off: patients aged <b>70 or over</b> should be <code>TRUE</code>.")
} else if (!exists("fit", envir = env, inherits = FALSE) ||
           !identical(names(env$fit$strata), c("old=FALSE", "old=TRUE"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "<code>survfit()</code> should give one curve per age group: put <code>old</code> on the right of the <code>~</code>.")
} else if (!grepl("times\\s*=\\s*365", .user_code)) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "One year is 365 days, so use <code>times = 365</code> in <code>summary()</code>.")
} else if (!inherits(.result, "survdiff") ||
           !identical(names(.result$n), c("old=FALSE", "old=TRUE"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "The last line should be the log-rank test comparing the two age groups: <code>survdiff()</code> with <code>~ old</code>.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE,
       message = "Correct! Older patients: median 283 days. Younger: 340 days. Log-rank p = 0.04. Now answer: is the difference statistically significant?")
}
```

## Interactive app: two-arm study simulator {#sec-app-km-sim}

Here we simulate a two-arm study where we know the truth. The dashed lines
are the **true** survival curves. The solid lines are the KM estimates from
one simulated sample. Change the sample size and seed to see how much KM
curves and log-rank p-values vary from sample to sample.

::: {.app}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof k2Scen = Inputs.radio(["Default", "Small study (20 per arm)", "Large study (150 per arm)", "No true effect (HR = 1)", "Short follow-up (6 months)", "Heavy drop-out"], {value: "Default", label: "Scenario"})
k2P = ({"Default": {}, "Small study (20 per arm)": {"n": 20}, "Large study (150 per arm)": {"n": 150}, "No true effect (HR = 1)": {"hr": 1}, "Short follow-up (6 months)": {"fu": 6}, "Heavy drop-out": {"drop": 0.08}})[k2Scen]
viewof k2 = Inputs.form({
  n:      Inputs.range([10, 500], {value: k2P.n ?? 60, step: 10, label: "Patients per arm"}),
  median: Inputs.range([3, 36], {value: k2P.median ?? 12, step: 1, label: "Control median (months)"}),
  hr:     Inputs.range([0.3, 1.5], {value: k2P.hr ?? 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "True hazard ratio (B vs A)"}),
  fu:     Inputs.range([6, 60], {value: k2P.fu ?? 30, step: 6, label: "Max follow-up (months)"}),
  drop:   Inputs.range([0, 0.1], {value: k2P.drop ?? 0.01, step: 0.005, label: "Drop-out rate (per month)"}),
  seed:   Inputs.range([1, 200], {value: k2P.seed ?? 1, step: 1, label: "Random seed (new study)"}),
  ci:     Inputs.toggle({label: "Show 95% CIs", value: k2P.ci ?? true})
}, {template: formGrid})
formGrid = inputs => html`<div class="form-grid">${Object.values(inputs)}</div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
k2sim = {
  const r = makeRandom(k2.seed);
  const lam0 = Math.LN2 / k2.median;
  const out = [];
  for (const [g, lam] of [["A (control)", lam0], ["B (treatment)", lam0 * k2.hr]]) {
    for (let i = 0; i < k2.n; i++) {
      const tE = r.exp(lam);
      const tC = Math.min(k2.fu * (0.5 + 0.5 * r.unif()), k2.drop > 0 ? r.exp(k2.drop) : Infinity);
      out.push({group: g, g: g.startsWith("B") ? 1 : 0, time: Math.min(tE, tC), event: tE <= tC ? 1 : 0});
    }
  }
  return out;
}
k2fits = ["A (control)", "B (treatment)"].flatMap(g => {
  const d = k2sim.filter(x => x.group === g);
  return kmFit(d.map(x => x.time), d.map(x => x.event)).map(r => ({...r, group: g}));
})
k2true = {
  const lam0 = Math.LN2 / k2.median, pts = [];
  for (let t = 0; t <= k2.fu; t += k2.fu / 100) {
    pts.push({time: t, surv: Math.exp(-lam0 * t), group: "A (control)"});
    pts.push({time: t, surv: Math.exp(-lam0 * k2.hr * t), group: "B (treatment)"});
  }
  return pts;
}
k2lr = logrank(k2sim.map(d => d.time), k2sim.map(d => d.event), k2sim.map(d => d.g))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  height: 340, y: {domain: [0, 1], grid: true, label: "Survival probability"},
  x: {label: "Months →", domain: [0, k2.fu]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["A (control)", "B (treatment)"], range: ["#E69F00", "#0072B2"]},
  marks: [
    k2.ci ? Plot.areaY(k2fits, {x: "time", y1: "lower", y2: "upper", fill: "group", fillOpacity: 0.15, curve: "step-after"}) : null,
    Plot.line(k2true, {x: "time", y: "surv", stroke: "group", strokeDasharray: "5,4", strokeOpacity: 0.8}),
    Plot.line(k2fits, {x: "time", y: "surv", stroke: "group", strokeWidth: 2.2, curve: "step-after"}),
    Plot.dot(k2fits.filter(r => r.ncens > 0), {x: "time", y: "surv", stroke: "group", symbol: "plus", r: 3})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const tbl = [];
  for (const g of ["A (control)", "B (treatment)"]) {
    const d = k2sim.filter(x => x.group === g);
    const f = k2fits.filter(r => r.group === g);
    const isA = g.startsWith("A");
    tbl.push({Arm: g, N: d.length, Events: d.filter(x => x.event).length,
      "Observed (O)": isA ? k2lr.O0 : k2lr.O1, "Expected (E)": (isA ? k2lr.E0 : k2lr.E1).toFixed(1),
      "KM median": isNaN(kmMedian(f)) ? "not reached" : kmMedian(f).toFixed(1),
      "True median": (k2.median / (isA ? 1 : k2.hr)).toFixed(1)});
  }
  return Inputs.table(tbl, {layout: "auto"});
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="font-size:1.05em">Log-rank test: χ² = <b>${k2lr.chisq.toFixed(2)}</b> on 1 df,
p = <b style="color:${k2lr.p < 0.05 ? '#0072B2' : '#D55E00'}">${k2lr.p < 0.0001 ? "< 0.0001" : k2lr.p.toFixed(4)}</b>
${k2lr.p < 0.05 ? "(significant at 5%)" : "(not significant at 5%)"}</p>`
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Things to try
For each one, **predict first**: decide what you expect to see, then pick the scenario and check. Committing to a prediction, even a wrong one, makes the result stick.

1. **Power.** **Predict:** with only 20 patients per arm and a real effect
   (HR = 0.6), how often will the log-rank test give p < 0.05? *Then* pick
   **Small study (20 per arm)** and step through several seeds. Compare with
   **Large study (150 per arm)**.
2. **No effect.** **Predict:** if the treatment does nothing, can the test
   still give p < 0.05? *Then* pick **No true effect (HR = 1)** and step
   through seeds.
3. **Censoring.** **Predict:** if follow-up stops at 6 months, what happens
   to the medians and the p-value? *Then* pick **Short follow-up (6
   months)**.
4. **The tail.** **Predict:** with many drop-outs, which part of the curves
   will be most uncertain? *Then* pick **Heavy drop-out**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answers: what you should see
1. **Power.** With 20 per arm, the true HR of 0.6 gives p < 0.05 in only
   about **1 seed in 5**. The chance that a study detects a real effect
   (p < 0.05) is called its **power**. Across 200 simulated studies, the
   power here was about 20%. A real effect is often missed in a small study. With 150 per arm,
   power is about **90%**. Notice also how much the 20-per-arm KM curves
   wander around the dashed true curves.
2. **No effect.** With HR = 1, about **5%** of seeds give p < 0.05. That's
   exactly what a 5% significance level means: these are false positives.
   If you click through 20 seeds you'll probably find one or two.
3. **Short follow-up.** With 6 months of follow-up, both medians are "not
   reached" (the control median is 12 months), there are only a handful of
   events, and power falls from about 55% to about 22% (at 60 per arm). The
   number of patients hasn't changed, only the number of **events**.
4. **High drop-out.** The risk table thins out quickly, so the confidence
   bands balloon at the right of the plot. On average the curves still
   follow the dashed truth, because random drop-out is *non-informative*.
   KM handles it correctly, but you get less precision.
:::

## Comparing more than two groups {#sec-pairwise}

With three or more groups, `survdiff()` gives an **omnibus** test. Its null
hypothesis is that *all* the survival curves are the same, so a small
p-value tells you that *at least one* group differs, but not which one.

The `lung` data record each patient's **ECOG performance status**, a score
of how well they manage daily activities (0 = fully active, higher = more
impaired). Only one patient scored 3, so we combine scores of 2 and 3 into
"2+":

```{r}
#| label: ecog-groups
lung <- lung |>
  mutate(ecog = factor(pmin(ph.ecog, 2), levels = 0:2,
                       labels = c("0 (active)", "1", "2+")))

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)     # medians by group
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-km-ecog
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan–Meier curves by ECOG performance status."
survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Days since enrolment")
```

Median survival falls from 394 days (ECOG 0) to 306 (ECOG 1) and 183
(ECOG 2+). (One patient has no ECOG score, so they are left out.) The
omnibus log-rank test:

```{r}
#| label: logrank-omnibus
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)
```

The omnibus test is clear ($\chi^2 = 19.0$ on 2 degrees of freedom,
$p < 0.001$). To find out *which* groups differ, compare each pair of
groups. With three groups there are three pairs. Running several tests
raises the chance of at least one false positive above 5%, so the p-values
are **adjusted** for multiple testing. The **Holm** method is a good
default. `pairwise_survdiff()` from the **survminer** package does all of
this:

```{r}
#| label: survminer-pairwise
library(survminer)
pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung,
                  p.adjust.method = "holm")
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## How to read this output
Each number is the Holm-adjusted p-value for one pair of groups. Find a
row and a column, e.g. *2+* (row) vs *0 (active)* (column), adjusted
p = 0.00009.

**Always set `p.adjust.method`.** If you leave it out,
`pairwise_survdiff()` uses a less strict adjustment (Benjamini–Hochberg),
and you'll get smaller p-values than these.
:::

Patients with ECOG 2+ had worse survival than both ECOG 0 (adjusted
p < 0.001) and ECOG 1 (adjusted p = 0.005). The difference between ECOG 0
and 1 is not significant after adjustment (p = 0.06).

To report *how big* the differences between groups are (hazard ratios), or
to test for a steady trend across ordered groups like these, you need a Cox
model. See @sec-cox-groups in the next chapter.

:::: {.optional}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Going further (optional): what `pairwise_survdiff()` does, and Holm vs BH
For each pair of groups, `pairwise_survdiff()` keeps only the patients in
those two groups and runs an ordinary two-group `survdiff()`. Then it adjusts
the p-values. The short function below does the same thing step by step.
It's in [`pairwise_logrank.R`](R/pairwise_logrank.R){download="pairwise_logrank.R"}
if you want it.

```{r}
#| label: pairwise-fn
#| file: R/pairwise_logrank.R
```

```{r}
#| label: pairwise-helper
pairwise_logrank(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)
```

The `p_adj` column matches `pairwise_survdiff()`.

- **Holm** (and Bonferroni) control the *family-wise error rate*: the
  chance of making *any* false-positive claim. Holm is always at least as
  powerful as Bonferroni.
- **Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)** controls the *false discovery rate*: the
  expected proportion of false positives among the comparisons you call
  significant. It's less strict, so its adjusted p-values are smaller.
:::
::::

**Good practice.** Plan your comparisons before you see the data: you often
don't need every pair. ("Each dose vs placebo" is 3 comparisons for 4 groups,
not 6.) Say which adjustment you used, and report survival estimates such as
medians for each group, not just p-values. A methods sentence might read:
*"Survival was compared between ECOG groups using the log-rank test, followed
by pairwise log-rank tests with Holm's correction, using the survival
[@survival-package] and survminer [@survminer] packages in R."* The
references come from `citation("survival")` and `citation("survminer")`.

## Reporting Kaplan–Meier results {#sec-km-reporting}

A good KM summary normally includes:

- the plot, **with a risk table** and censoring marks;
- the number of events and number at risk in each group;
- median survival with a 95% CI (or "not reached");
- survival at clinically meaningful times (e.g. 1-year survival) with CIs;
- the log-rank p-value, *and* an effect size such as a hazard ratio from a
  Cox model (Chapter 3).

### Writing it up

A sentence template you can adapt:

> Median survival was **[X]** days (95% CI **[a]** to **[b]**) in **[group 1]**
> and **[Y]** days (95% CI **[c]** to **[d]**) in **[group 2]**. At
> **[time]**, **[p1]**% (95% CI …) of **[group 1]** and **[p2]**% (95% CI …)
> of **[group 2]** were still alive. Survival differed between the groups
> (log-rank test, $\chi^2$ = **[value]**, **[df]** df, p = **[value]**).

Filled in for the `lung` data:

> Median survival was 426 days (95% CI 348 to 550) in women and 270 days
> (95% CI 212 to 310) in men. At one year, 53% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of women
> and 34% (95% CI 26% to 43%) of men were still alive. Survival differed
> between the sexes (log-rank test, $\chi^2$ = 10.3, 1 df, p = 0.001).

The **gtsummary** package's `tbl_survfit()` can produce these numbers as a
table.

## Quick quiz {.unnumbered}

Choose an answer to each question. You'll get instant feedback and can change your answer as often as you like.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz([
 {
  "q": "Survival times are <code>5, 8+, 10, 12</code>. What is the Kaplan–Meier estimate of S(10)?",
  "options": [
   "0.500",
   "0.375",
   "0.250",
   "0.667"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "At t = 5: 4 at risk, 1 death, so S = 3/4 = 0.75. The patient censored at 8 leaves. At t = 10: 2 at risk, 1 death, so S = 0.75 × 1/2 = 0.375.",
  "hints": [
   "That's what you'd get by treating 8+ as if it weren't there at all (2 of 4 died by t = 10). KM keeps the censored patient in the risk set until time 8.",
   "",
   "That would mean 3 of 4 had died, but the patient censored at 8 didn't die.",
   "Check the risk set at t = 10: only 2 patients are left, not 3."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "R reports the median survival in one group as <code>NA</code>. What does that mean?",
  "options": [
   "The data contain missing values",
   "Survival never fell to 50% during follow-up",
   "The median is zero",
   "The group is too small to analyse"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "The median is the first time S(t) ≤ 0.5. If the curve never gets that low, the median is 'not reached'. Report it that way.",
  "hints": [
   "Missing values are dropped before fitting. They don't cause an NA median.",
   "",
   "A median of 0 would mean half the group had the event immediately.",
   "Even small groups get a median if the curve passes 0.5."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "A log-rank test gives p = 0.001. What can you conclude?",
  "options": [
   "The hazard ratio is 0.001",
   "There's strong evidence that the survival curves differ, but nothing about how large the difference is",
   "There's a 99.9% chance the treatment works",
   "The difference is clinically important"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "The log-rank test only gives a p-value. To describe the size of the difference, report a hazard ratio, median survival or survival at fixed times.",
  "hints": [
   "A p-value is not an effect size.",
   "",
   "A p-value isn't the probability that a hypothesis is true.",
   "Statistical significance says nothing about clinical importance."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "Two KM curves cross at about 1 year. What's the main concern for the log-rank test?",
  "options": [
   "None, because the log-rank test makes no assumptions",
   "It may have low power, because early and late differences cancel out",
   "It can't be computed when curves cross",
   "It will always give p < 0.05"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "The log-rank test is most powerful when hazards are proportional. When curves cross, the differences before and after the crossing partly cancel, so a real difference can be missed.",
  "hints": [
   "It is non-parametric, but it is most powerful under proportional hazards.",
   "",
   "It can always be computed. It just may not be informative.",
   "If anything, crossing curves make a significant result *less* likely."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "A log-rank test comparing 4 groups gives p = 0.002. What should you do next?",
  "options": [
   "Conclude that all four groups differ from each other",
   "Follow up with pairwise comparisons (adjusting the p-values, e.g. Holm), or pre-planned comparisons, and report HRs with CIs",
   "Run all six pairwise tests at the 5% level without adjustment",
   "Nothing more: the omnibus p-value is enough to report"
  ],
  "answer": 1,
  "why": "The omnibus test says at least one curve differs, not which. Adjusted pairwise tests, or a few pre-planned comparisons, answer that question, and HRs show how big the differences are.",
  "hints": [
   "The omnibus test only says that *at least one* group differs.",
   "",
   "Six unadjusted tests push the chance of at least one false positive to around 26%.",
   "Readers will want to know which groups differ, and by how much."
  ]
 }
])
```

## Hint 1

## Solution
```r
fit <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran)
fit |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Days")
fit
```

Median survival was 118 days (squamous), 51 (small cell), 51 (adeno) and
156 (large). Small cell and adeno tumours have much shorter survival.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_veteran_km
#| check: true
r <- .result
if (!inherits(r, "survfit") || is.null(r$strata)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line the fitted KM object, e.g. <code>fit</code>, where <code>fit &lt;- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran)</code>.")
} else if (length(r$strata) != 4 || !all(grepl("celltype", names(r$strata)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Group the curves by <code>celltype</code>: there should be four of them.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Medians: 118 days (squamous), 51 (small cell), 51 (adeno) and 156 (large).")
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_veteran
#| caption: "Exercise 2.1, part 2: comparing cell types"
# 1. Log-rank test


# 2. Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons (last line)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_veteran"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1
These are the same functions used for ECOG in @sec-pairwise: `survdiff()`, then `pairwise_survdiff()`. Use `data = veteran` and `~ celltype`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_veteran"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2
```r
pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran,
                  p.adjust.method = ______)
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_veteran"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran)
pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran,
                  p.adjust.method = "holm")
```

The omnibus test has 3 degrees of freedom (4 groups − 1). Its null
hypothesis is that all four curves are identical, and it is clearly rejected
($\chi^2 = 25.4$, $p < 0.001$). The pairwise tests show two clusters:
squamous and large cell have similar survival (adjusted p = 0.73), as do
small cell and adeno (adjusted p = 0.76). Every comparison *between* the
clusters is significant.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_veteran
#| check: true
code_lines <- strsplit(.user_code, "\n")[[1]]
# an omnibus survdiff() call on celltype (not pairwise_survdiff)
has_omnibus <- any(grepl("(^|[^_A-Za-z.])survdiff\\s*\\(", code_lines) &
                   grepl("celltype", code_lines))
if (!has_omnibus) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
       message = "Include the omnibus log-rank test: <code>survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran)</code>.")
} else if (!inherits(.result, "pairwise.htest")) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = "Make the <b>last line</b> the pairwise comparisons, using <code>pairwise_survdiff()</code>.")
} else if (!identical(.result$p.adjust.method, "holm")) {
  list(correct = FALSE,
       message = paste0("Nearly there. Your pairwise tests used the <code>", .result$p.adjust.method,
                        "</code> adjustment. Set <code>p.adjust.method = \"holm\"</code>."))
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE,
       message = "Correct! Squamous and large cell are similar (adjusted p = 0.73), as are small cell and adeno (0.76). Every comparison between these two clusters is significant.")
}
```

## Summary

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Key points
- The **KM estimator** multiplies together the chances of surviving each event time: $1 - d/n$. A censored patient leaves the risk set without causing a drop.
- Report KM curves **with a risk table**, plus median survival (or 'not reached') and survival at chosen times, each with a 95% CI.
- The **hazard** is the event rate among people still at risk. A **hazard ratio** compares two groups' hazards.
- The **log-rank test** checks whether survival curves differ. It gives only a p-value, works best when the hazard ratio is constant, and doesn't adjust for other variables.
- With three or more groups, follow a significant omnibus test with **pairwise tests adjusted for multiple testing** (e.g. Holm). Always set `p.adjust.method`.
:::

**Answering the question.** Yes. Median survival was 426 days for women and 270 days for men. One year after enrolment, about 53% of women and 34% of men were still alive. The log-rank test gave p = 0.001. How *much* lower women's risk was, and whether that holds after accounting for age and fitness, is the next chapter's question.

## Further reading

All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise. The whole
book's reading list, grouped by topic, is in @sec-further-reading.

- @bland1998km: A one-page explanation of the Kaplan–Meier method, with a worked example.
- @bland2004logrank: A one-page explanation of how the log-rank test works, from the same series.
- @clark2003: The Kaplan–Meier and log-rank sections of this paper cover the same ground in more detail, including how to present results.
